topic: Evals as infrastructure: eval sets, LLM-as-judge, human review, CI gates
why: At the end of every pilot an FDE has to answer one question in front of the customer's engineering lead and their exec sponsor: how do you know it works? Without a labelled set you own, per-class numbers with intervals, and a gate that blocks regressions before merge, the honest answer is a demo and a feeling - so the pilot converts on trust rather than evidence, and the first bad week kills it. Evals are also the only mechanism that lets you change a prompt, swap a model or ship a retrieval improvement on a customer's production path without gambling with their data, and the only artefact that turns 'it got worse this month' into a specific class, a specific date and a specific commit.
prerequisites: The prompt-as-code machinery from 'Prompt engineering as code' (topic 46): versioned prompt files with pinned model snapshots, the deterministic assertion ladder, a committed baseline.json, and an eval runner with response caching, bounded concurrency and a USD ceiling. This topic layers labels, judges and statistics on top of that runner - it does not rebuild it.

Classification metrics at working depth: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, class imbalance, and enough pandas/numpy to pivot a results file by class and tag. Have scikit-learn, scipy and statsmodels installed and know how to call them.

LLM mechanics from topic 45: run-to-run variance at temperature 0, dated snapshots versus moving aliases, and the fact that fluency and correctness are close to uncorrelated - which is the entire reason a judge needs validating.
pytest and GitHub Actions from topics 35 and 18: parametrize and fixtures, required status checks, path filters, workflow_dispatch, artifacts, and posting a sticky comment on a pull request.

A real system with real traffic: DefenderMate's classifier plus several hundred stored production traces (the llm_calls and audit_log tables from topic 30), and commitment from one domain expert for about four hours of labelling and adjudication. Without a domain expert this topic degenerates into statistics homework.
RAG basics from topic 49 if you intend to evaluate a retrieval path - chunking, top-k retrieval, and the difference between a retrieval failure and a generation failure.

subtopics.name: The three eval levels and what each one can actually prove
subtopics.learn: Separate Level 1 (assertions on a single component: schema validity, exact match, retrieval recall@k - cheap, deterministic, runs on every commit), Level 2 (human or judge review of a whole trace, i.e. the output the user actually sees, including multi-step agent runs), and Level 3 (production outcome metrics: acceptance rate, edit distance between the model's draft and the analyst's final text, escalation rate, task completion). A Level 1 pass never licenses a Level 3 claim, and this is the most common way an FDE oversells a pilot. Write the mapping down per feature: for DefenderMate, 'retrieval recall@10' is Level 1, 'the finding summary is defensible from the evidence' is Level 2, 'the analyst accepted it without editing' is Level 3. Decide explicitly which level owns the release decision for each feature before you build anything.

resource.label: Hamel Husain - Your AI Product Needs Evals

subtopics.name: Error analysis: open-coding a sample of real traces
subtopics.learn: Before any metric exists, pull a stratified sample of 50-100 real production traces, read each end to end, and write one free-text sentence naming the first thing that goes wrong - no categories, no scores, no 1-5 ratings. Do the first 30 yourself sitting next to the domain expert; delegating this step is why most eval efforts measure the wrong thing. Stop when 10-15 consecutive traces produce no new kind of note (theoretical saturation), which usually happens well before 100. The deliverable of this step is a spreadsheet with trace_id, input, output and a notes column - deliberately not a number.

resource.label: Hamel Husain - A Field Guide to Rapidly Improving AI Products (the error analysis process)

subtopics.name: Axial coding: notes into a counted failure taxonomy
subtopics.learn: Cluster the free-text notes into 8-15 mutually exclusive, named failure categories - you can have a model propose the clustering, but you arbitrate the boundaries and the names. Count each category and sort by frequency multiplied by business cost; the distribution is almost always brutally skewed, with two categories accounting for over half the errors, which is what tells you where to spend the next fortnight. Every category then gets exactly one disposition: a deterministic assertion, a dedicated judge, or an explicitly documented known limitation in the customer report. Re-run open plus axial coding monthly on fresh traces - a frozen taxonomy is how you stop noticing new failure kinds.

resource.label: Hamel Husain & Shreya Shankar - AI Evals FAQ: axial coding into a failure taxonomy

subtopics.name: Building the 200-case set: sampling frame, stratification, provenance
subtopics.learn: Write the sampling frame down before you sample: which tenants, which date range, which document types, which languages, and what you deliberately excluded. Stratify across every dimension you intend to report on and oversample rare-but-expensive classes so each class has enough support to produce a usable interval - 8 examples of your most important class is not a measurement. Fix the case schema as {id, inputs{}, expected{}, class, tags[], source, labeller, labelled_at, notes} and populate from exactly three streams: stratified production traffic, every customer-reported bug converted into a case on the day it is reported, and deliberate degenerate/adversarial inputs. Mark synthetic cases with source='synthetic' and keep them under about a quarter of the set, or you end up measuring your own imagination.

resource.label: OpenAI Platform docs - Evals guide

subtopics.name: Splits, contamination and freezing a held-out test set
subtopics.learn: Split stratified into dev and test (roughly 60/40 at this size), iterate only against dev, and look at test only at release. Any example used as a few-shot in the production prompt or inside a judge prompt is banned from both splits - contamination here inflates the number you will quote to a customer. Keep a counter of how many times the test set has been evaluated: every look leaks information, and after twenty looks it is a dev set with a fancy name. Version the dataset (dataset_id plus a content hash recorded in every results file), rotate fresh production cases in quarterly, and archive rather than delete old versions so historical scores stay interpretable.

resource.label: GitHub - openai/evals (eval registry, dataset and JSONL case format)

subtopics.name: Labelling guidelines, a single label owner, and a fast review UI
subtopics.learn: Write a one-to-two page guideline containing a decision procedure, a worked example at the boundary of every class, and explicit tie-break rules; version it in Git alongside the dataset. Name one principal domain expert who owns the label definition and settles disputes - labels defined by committee drift, and drifting labels silently move every metric. Build the fastest possible review surface: keyboard-only, one keystroke per class, input and model output side by side, writing straight into a table with labeller and timestamp. Do the arithmetic before you start: 200 cases at 30 seconds each is 100 minutes and will get done; at 3 minutes each it is 10 hours and will not.

resource.label: GitHub - HumanSignal/label-studio (annotation interfaces and label config)

subtopics.name: Inter-annotator agreement and the ceiling it sets on your metrics
subtopics.learn: Double-label 20-30% of the set with a second annotator and compute Cohen's kappa - never raw percent agreement, because with 90% negatives two coin-flippers agree 82% of the time. Read the number as a verdict on your guideline, not on the annotators: below about 0.4 the guideline is broken and must be rewritten before another label is collected; 0.6-0.8 is workable; a suspiciously perfect 1.0 usually means you are labelling something trivial that did not need a model. Human-human agreement is the hard ceiling on any score you can claim for the model, so quote it in the report. Adjudicate every disagreement with the label owner and fold each resolution back into the guideline as a new worked example.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score

subtopics.name: Per-class metrics: confusion matrix, macro vs micro, support
subtopics.learn: Report a confusion matrix plus per-class precision, recall and F1 with support - a single blended accuracy on imbalanced data is a number that structurally cannot go down and therefore carries no information. Know precisely what the averages hide: macro-F1 weights every class equally so rare classes dominate the mean, micro-F1 equals accuracy in the single-label case, and weighted-F1 is the one that lets a broken rare class disappear behind a healthy common one. Use classification_report(y_true, y_pred, labels=ALL_CLASSES, zero_division=0) and always pass labels explicitly, otherwise a class the model never predicts silently vanishes from the table instead of showing as a row of zeros. For multi-label extraction, compute set precision/recall per document and micro-average across the corpus, and state which one you used.

resource.label: scikit-learn User Guide - Metrics and scoring

subtopics.name: Operating points: PR curve, cost-weighted thresholds, abstention
subtopics.learn: A scored classifier is not one system but a family of them; pick the operating point deliberately from a precision-recall curve computed on dev and confirm it on test, rather than inheriting whatever threshold the first prototype used. Choose it in the customer's cost units: for DefenderMate a missed critical finding is a breach-notification conversation while a false positive costs an analyst three seconds to dismiss, so gate on recall at a fixed acceptable precision and say so out loud. Add a third outcome - abstain and route to human review - and then always report coverage alongside accuracy-on-covered, because a system that answers 40% of cases perfectly is a different product from one that answers all of them. Check calibration before trusting any score: LLM verbal confidences are usually not calibrated probabilities, so bin them and plot observed correctness per bin before you threshold on 0.8.

resource.label: scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve

subtopics.name: Confidence intervals and how many examples you actually need
subtopics.learn: Every eval score is an estimate from a sample, so report an interval with it: proportion_confint(count, nobs, method='wilson') rather than the normal approximation, which misbehaves near 0 and 1 and at small n. Internalise the scale so you can do it in a customer meeting: about 50 examples of a class gives roughly plus or minus 13 points at 95%, 200 gives about plus or minus 7, and resolving a 3-point difference needs thousands. The direct consequence is what your 200-case set can and cannot support - it can prove 'this class is badly broken' and 'this is broadly working at the level we agreed', but it cannot prove that 94.1% beats 92.8% on its own. Put n and the interval next to every number in every report, and refuse to ship a table without them.

resource.label: statsmodels - proportion_confint (Wilson and other binomial intervals)

subtopics.name: Comparing two systems: paired bootstrap, McNemar, multiple comparisons
subtopics.learn: Run both variants over identical cases and compare per-case outcomes rather than two independent aggregate scores; pairing removes case-difficulty variance and is exactly why n=200 can detect changes an unpaired comparison would need thousands for. For binary correctness use McNemar's test on the discordant cells (b = old right and new wrong, c = old wrong and new right), with the exact binomial version when b+c is under about 25 - note that the concordant cells contribute nothing, so a change touching 6 cases is weak evidence no matter how big the set. For any other metric, use a paired bootstrap: resample case indices with replacement 10,000 times, recompute the delta each time, and report the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles. When you slice by twelve classes you are running twelve tests, so either apply Benjamini-Hochberg or state plainly that the slice view is exploratory.

resource.label: statsmodels - McNemar test for paired nominal data

subtopics.name: LLM-as-judge: the three modes, and when not to use one at all
subtopics.learn: Know the modes and their reliability ordering: pairwise comparison (A vs B, the most reliable signal and how arena-style rankings work, but yields no absolute number), reference-based grading (compare against a gold answer, closest to a deterministic check), and direct scoring against a rubric (most convenient, least stable). The governing rule: never use a judge where a deterministic check exists - exact and normalised match, set F1, JSON schema validity, regex must-contain/must-not-contain, SQL execution equality, or citation-span containment are all cheaper, free to run and perfectly reproducible. Judges earn their keep only on genuinely open-ended properties: is this summary faithful to the evidence, is the tone appropriate for a regulator, does this actually answer the question asked. Reject any request for an undefined 1-10 quality scale; a binary verdict with a written definition is both more reliable and more actionable.

resource.label: Eugene Yan - Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLM-Evaluators (direct scoring vs pairwise vs reference-based)

subtopics.name: Writing the judge: one failure mode, binary rubric, critique-then-verdict
subtopics.learn: Build one judge per category in your failure taxonomy, each testing a single narrowly-defined criterion and returning pass/fail - a single omnibus 'quality' judge is unstable across runs and tells you nothing you can act on. Structure the prompt as role, the exact criterion with its boundary cases spelled out, then 3-6 few-shot examples drawn from your own human-labelled disagreements including near-miss failures, and force reasoning before commitment by ordering the output schema as {"reasoning": ..., "verdict": "pass"|"fail"} so the verdict token is generated after the critique. Give the judge exactly what a human reviewer needs and nothing more - input, output, and the reference if one exists - because extra context invites the judge to invent criteria. Pin the judge's model snapshot and version the judge prompt like any other prompt (topic 46): changing the judge retroactively changes every number you have ever reported.

resource.label: Claude docs - Define your success criteria (test and evaluate)

subtopics.name: Validating the judge against humans, and correcting its estimates
subtopics.learn: A judge is itself a classifier and must be evaluated as one: assemble a set of judge decisions with human ground truth, then compute per-class true positive rate and true negative rate plus Cohen's kappa against the human - not 'judge accuracy', which on a skewed set is meaningless. Iterate the judge prompt against this validation set until kappa clears a stated floor (0.7 is a reasonable target) and accept that you cannot beat your own human-human agreement. Once TPR and TNR are known you can debias the judge's estimate on unlabelled data with p_true = (p_observed - (1 - TNR)) / (TPR + TNR - 1), which is the difference between reporting a judge's opinion and reporting a measurement. Re-validate on a fresh 50-case sample whenever the judge model snapshot changes, the judge prompt changes, or the input distribution shifts - all three happen more often than teams expect.

resource.label: Hamel Husain - Using LLM-as-a-Judge for Evaluation (critique shadowing: aligning the judge with a domain expert)

subtopics.name: Judge pathologies: position, verbosity, self-preference, score clustering
subtopics.learn: Position bias in pairwise judging is large and systematic, so always run both orderings and count only the verdicts that survive the swap, treating flips as ties and reporting the flip rate as a health metric. Verbosity bias means longer answers score higher independent of quality, so either control for length or report token counts next to scores. Self-preference means a model favours its own generations, so never let the same model family be both generator and judge for a release decision - use a different vendor or at minimum a different family and say which in the report. Score clustering is why 1-10 rubrics fail in practice: judges pile verdicts on 7 and 8 and never use the extremes, so a two-point 'improvement' is inside the noise; this is the strongest practical argument for binary rubrics.

resource.label: arXiv - Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al.)

subtopics.name: Graders for retrieval and open-ended output
subtopics.learn: Decompose a RAG answer into separately measurable properties instead of grading it as one blob: retrieval quality (recall@k, MRR, nDCG against a labelled query-to-chunk set), groundedness/faithfulness (split the answer into atomic claims and check each against the retrieved context), answer relevance, and context precision. Prefer mechanical citation checking where you can get it - require the model to emit chunk ids and verify the quoted span appears verbatim in that chunk - over asking a judge whether the text 'is faithful'. This decomposition is what lets you attribute a score drop to the retriever rather than the prompt, which ties directly back to topic 49; without it you will spend a week rewriting a prompt to fix a chunking bug.

resource.label: GitHub - explodinggradients/ragas (RAG evaluation metrics)

subtopics.name: The harness: promptfoo config, caching, and a results schema you own
subtopics.learn: Learn the promptfoo config surface: providers, prompts, tests with vars and assert blocks, assertion types (equals, contains, is-json with a schema, javascript/python custom asserts, llm-rubric and model-graded variants), defaultTest for shared assertions, and per-test thresholds. Drive it with promptfoo eval -c evals/classifier.yaml --output results.json, use --no-cache for the authoritative pre-release run, and promptfoo view for local triage of individual failures. Whatever tool you pick, insist on the same invariants: one row per case in the results file (case id, class, expected, actual, each assertion outcome, tokens, latency, USD), deterministic case ordering, response caching keyed on model plus rendered prompt plus params, bounded concurrency with backoff on 429, and a hard spend ceiling that aborts the run. Emit your own stable results.jsonl schema on top of whatever the tool produces, so your reporting and history survive migrating harnesses - which you will do at least once.

resource.label: promptfoo documentation - Introduction

subtopics.name: The CI gate: tiers, per-class floors, noise budget, and staying required
subtopics.learn: Run two tiers: a smoke suite of about 30 stratified cases finishing in under two minutes as a required check on pull_request behind path filters, and the full 200-case suite nightly on schedule plus workflow_dispatch. Gate on per-class floors and per-class deltas rather than a global mean - fail when any class's recall falls more than two sigma below its baseline, where sigma comes from actually running the suite five times against an unchanged system rather than from a number someone liked. Gate the non-accuracy budgets in the same job: p95 latency, tokens per case, and USD per 1,000 cases, so a change that doubles cost fails like any other regression. Make the failure legible - sticky PR comment with the per-class table, the delta against baseline, and the ids of the cases that flipped in each direction, plus results.jsonl as an artifact - because an unexplained red X gets overridden twice and then removed from required checks, and a gate that is not required is a runbook paragraph.

resource.label: GitHub Actions documentation

subtopics.name: The production loop: online scoring, review queue, uncertainty sampling
subtopics.learn: An offline set decays the moment the customer changes what they send you, so sample production continuously: run the cheap judges online over a 1-5% sample plus 100% of high-risk classes, attach the scores to the trace, and alert on the failure rate over a window rather than on individual failures. Build a human review queue prioritised by uncertainty (scores near the operating threshold), disagreement (judge versus deterministic check, or two models disagreeing), and business impact - and make every human decision write a new labelled case with source='review_queue', which is how the eval set grows without a labelling sprint. Instrument implicit feedback as well as explicit: whether the analyst edited the draft and by how much, dismissed the finding, or escalated it, because thumbs up/down has both terrible response rates and worse calibration. Drift detection and the rollout mechanics live in topics 57 and 58; here you are building the label supply that feeds them.

resource.label: Langfuse docs - Annotation Queues (prioritised human review of production traces)

subtopics.name: The eval report the customer can forward to their exec
subtopics.learn: Write one page that an engineering lead and a non-technical sponsor can both read: what was measured, on how many examples, sampled how and from what window; a per-class table with precision, recall, support and 95% intervals; the confusion matrix; the top three failure categories with counts and one real example each; what changed since the last report; and an explicit section on what is not measured. State the chosen operating point and the human-agreement ceiling, so nobody expects 99% from a task where two experts agree 85% of the time. Frame the target as an SLO with an error budget rather than a promise of perfection - that framing is what converts an argument about a single bad output into a conversation about a budget - and never publish a number without n and an interval beside it.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

outcomes: You can produce a 200-case labelled set for DefenderMate with a written sampling frame, at least 20% double-labelled, a reported Cohen's kappa, and every case carrying source, labeller and labelled_at provenance.

You can report per-class precision, recall and F1 with support and 95% Wilson intervals plus a confusion matrix, and can explain in one sentence why you refuse to answer 'what's the accuracy?' with a single number.

You can state whether the difference between two prompt or model versions is real: paired run over identical cases, McNemar or paired bootstrap, an interval on the delta, and the sample size that would be needed to detect the effect the customer cares about.

You can build an LLM judge for one named failure mode and show its TPR, TNR and kappa against human labels on a held-out set of judge decisions, then quote the bias-corrected estimate rather than the raw judge pass rate.

You can make CI fail a pull request on a per-class recall regression beyond two sigma, with the flipped case ids named in the failure output and a sticky per-class score comment, with the smoke tier finishing under two minutes.

You can run an error-analysis session over 50 real traces and finish with a counted, mutually exclusive failure taxonomy in which the top two categories account for the majority of errors, each with an assigned disposition.
You can choose and defend an operating point from a precision-recall curve in the customer's cost units, including an abstain path, and report coverage next to accuracy-on-covered.
You can hand the customer a one-page eval report they forward to their exec unedited, including the section listing what is explicitly not measured.
failureModes: The eval set was assembled from cases the current system already passes, so it reads 97% every run, provides zero signal on every pull request, and the first genuinely new failure is still discovered by the customer's analyst.

A single blended accuracy figure hides that the rarest and most contractually important class has recall of 0.3 on 11 examples, and it stays hidden until the quarterly review when someone asks for the breakdown.

The judge is written, eyeballed on five examples and shipped without ever being scored against human labels, so a 'faithfulness: 92%' number goes into a QBR deck while the judge is in fact passing every fluent answer regardless of evidence.

The judge model is silently upgraded or its prompt is tweaked mid-quarter, so every historical score shifts and the longitudinal improvement chart in the customer report is entirely an artefact of the measuring instrument.
Two annotators labelled without a written guideline, kappa comes out at 0.35, and three weeks of prompt iteration turns out to have been fitting noise in the labels rather than improving the system.

Test-set cases leak into the production prompt's few-shot block (or into the judge's few-shots), so the headline score is measured on the system's own worked examples and does not survive contact with the customer's next batch of documents.

The CI gate is set exactly at the baseline with no noise allowance, produces four false failures in a fortnight, gets quietly removed from required checks, and now the only thing standing between a prompt edit and the customer's production data is code review.
interviewQuestions: A customer asks 'how do you know your classifier works?' You have two weeks and one domain expert who can give you four hours total. Walk me through exactly what you build, in what order, what number you put in front of them at the end, and what you explicitly refuse to claim.

Your eval says 94% accuracy and the customer's analysts say it's wrong all the time. Both statements are true. Explain how that happens mechanically, and tell me how you find out which of the two matters for renewal.

Design an LLM-as-judge for 'is this finding summary faithful to the retrieved evidence'. Then convince a sceptical staff engineer that the judge itself is trustworthy - and tell me what you do if it agrees with your human labeller only 65% of the time.

You change a prompt and the score moves from 91.5% to 93.0% on 200 labelled cases. Is that an improvement? Show me the actual arithmetic that answers it, and tell me what would be different in your answer if the move had been 91.5% to 96.0%.

Design the eval CI gate for a customer-facing extraction pipeline end to end: what runs on every PR versus nightly, what the thresholds are and how you derived the numbers, what stops it costing four hundred dollars a day, and what specifically prevents the team from marking it non-required after the third false failure.

You inherit a system with no evals, no labels and 40,000 stored production traces. What do you do on day one? Be concrete about how you sample, what you write down, who you sit with, and what artefact you have at the end of the week.

The customer wants a single 'quality score' out of 10 on their dashboard, refreshed daily. Explain what you push back on, what you offer instead, and how you make whatever number you do publish stable enough to trend over six months without the instrument itself drifting.
proofOfWork: A public repository, `defendermate-evals`, that a stranger can clone and run end to end in five minutes with `make eval` against a recorded-response fixture mode requiring no API key, so a reviewer can reproduce every number in the README for free. It contains the frozen 200-case dataset as JSONL with the schema above (real cases scrubbed or synthesised, `source` distinguishing production, bug-report and adversarial origins), the versioned `LABELLING_GUIDE.md` with worked boundary examples, and an `agreement/` directory holding the double-labelled subset plus the script that computes Cohen's kappa and prints the adjudication log for every disagreement. It ships the failure taxonomy as `TAXONOMY.md` with counts from a real open-coding session over 50 traces and a disposition column mapping each category to a deterministic assertion, a judge, or a documented limitation; a `judges/` package with one binary judge per open-ended category, each pinned to a dated model snapshot and accompanied by its own validation set of human-labelled judge decisions and a reported TPR/TNR/kappa table plus the bias-corrected pass rate; and a `stats.py` implementing Wilson intervals, McNemar and the paired bootstrap, with a test that fails if any published number in the README lacks an interval. The GitHub Actions workflow runs the 30-case smoke tier on `pull_request` behind path filters and posts a sticky per-class delta comment, with the repository history showing at least one real PR where the gate failed on a single class's recall, the comment naming the flipped case ids, and the follow-up commit that fixed it. Finally, `REPORT.md` is the customer-facing one-pager - per-class table with support and intervals, confusion matrix, top three failure categories with examples, the human-agreement ceiling, the chosen operating point and coverage, and a 'what this does not measure' section - rendered from the results file by a script, so it can never drift from the run that produced it.
